story: For four years, Sweden was governed by a centre-right coalition that depended on the votes of the Sweden Democrats, a party with roots in the neo-Nazi movement that became the country's second largest. It was a historic break in a country long seen as Europe's model of social democracy, and the government took a hard line on immigration and gang crime. In September, Swedes narrowly reversed it, and then found that winning was the easy part.

In the 13 September election, the four left-leaning parties won 176 of 349 seats against 173 for Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's bloc, and the Sweden Democrats lost ground, putting Sweden at odds with the far-right rise across much of Europe (L'Orient-Le Jour). Kristersson resigned on 17 September, and the speaker asked Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson, Sweden's first woman prime minister in 2021-22, to form a government (Euronews). Her bloc was fractured: the Centre Party and the Left Party disagree sharply. On 28 September, after the Left Party backed a centre-right candidate for speaker, Andersson said there was "currently no possibility" for her to form a government (Reuters via Oman Observer). The speaker can put up to four candidates to a vote; if all fail, Sweden must hold a new election. Kristersson stays on as caretaker.
briefing.power: A constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system of "negative parliamentarism": a prime minister takes office unless an absolute majority of the 349-seat Riksdag votes against. King Carl XVI Gustaf is ceremonial.
briefing.holders: Caretaker Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson (Moderates), while government formation continues.
